review: One of the BEST cyoa games!
Very atmospheric game with a highly reactive plot.

More of a "Meh" reccomendation.
It is a decent CYOA, with good length, seemingly a lot of options and a lot of very interesting adventure "hooks". However it is marred by a noticeable amount of syntax and grammar, as well as continuity errors. The game regularly assumes, or at least describes, little actions that you didn't undertake - and that already in your very first playthrough, which is a real shame, because it ruins the otherwise quite well done immersion into the story and setting as a whole.

The game seems to present a lot of options and choices, which is much appreciated, however the pacing and the implementation of the "game mechanics" are inconsistent at times. Sometimes you are presented with options to ask about topics and you have an infinite amount of time to ask about all presented options, which makes these sections feel arbitrary and plotting, especially when other times you make a choice and get thrown into something new entirely, without having been signposted, or even having the option of backing out.

Which brings me to another point of TRULY DIRE CRITIQUE for me: The interludes at the start of a chapter, where you go around shopping in your little town are horribly designed and single handedly ruin the immersion of the game for me, wouldn't the following chapter content be as good as it thankfully is.
You get to visit shops and improve your gear, however there is NO OPTION to back out of a selected item of interest - if you have money and ask the Blacksmith about special weaponry, you MUST choose one of the weapons to buy, whether you want them or not - leading me to being forced to buy a knife on my sharpshooting Marshall. Furthermore dialogue and options repeat inbetween visits, so you find yourself visiting the gunsmith in every single chapter and clicking on the "Talk about Explosives" Option, not because you ever would to get to BUY some explosives of any kind, no, but because it plainly gives you a stat boost, providing the same lines of dialogue each time. This happens for a variety of vendors in time. It's honestly a shame, as it ruins the aforementioned immersion and feels like an obligatory and opaque grind for stats. 
Talking about stats - unfortunately the "game" part of this CYOA has it's problems as well, since impactful choices have little or no signposting as to what they do, or what stats they might refer to. A brief example: I found myself fighting an antagonist, the game gave me the otpion of basically going into a gunfight, going into a brawling/knife fighting situation and asking him to surrender, I asked him to surrender, he didn't, so we went for a gunfight. The game gave me the option of then shooting the man in the chest, the head, the hand or his gun. My character has a very high sharpshooting stat and a decently high gunfighting stat, so I evaluated the options thinking that shooting the gun (the smallest target) is the most difficult option and has potential drawbacks of fighting the antagonist in melee, which my character is not apt at doing, same goes for shooting him in the hand and shooting him in the chest is a more easy option for gunfighting - so I opted for the head, since I am as mentioned a very good sharpshooter. Guess what - I died. I reloaded and shot at the revolver - it worked. Why is shooting the head somehow more difficult than shooting a gun out of his hand? Either way the game does not elaborate on which option pertains to which skill, how high your skill might need to be (could say: IT IS A DIFFICULT SHOT TO MAKE), or what might happen if it succeeds, or fails.

All in all this is a decent adventure, with great set pieces and adventure ideas, that tragically gets undermined by poor signposting and generally poor game mechanic implementation, as well as the occasional mistake in prose.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 549:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (10/10)

Well, g*ddamn. Usually I have an idea of how my review will go as I play a game, but for [i]Tin Star,[/i] I was just enthralled. I had literally no thoughts, head empty, because I was so focused on finishing the game. I’ve read at least 30 Interactive Fiction games, but[i] Tin Star[/i] has shot up to the best of the best. You are strong-armed (long story) into being a newly-appointed U.S. marshal of Lander County, a wild place of land around Nevada. For ten incredible chapters, you act as the law. The unique, thorough mechanics system is happily married to detailed, historically-accurate writing. I haven’t even mentioned the two incredible female ROs, and the “conspiracy whose deadly web stretches from San Francisco to New York City.” I didn’t give the blurb much thought—it’s just trying to build hype—but ... you know how in[i] Ace Attorney[/i] you have random plot threads that all coalesce at the end? And how the theme song kicks in, you look back at the evidence, and everything makes sense all of a sudden? Yeah. That’s how[i] Tin Sta[/i]r ends. I’m surprised the Steam page says it’s the first hosted game published; it sets the bar so high, even almost 10 years later.

[b][h2]Pros:[/h2][/b]
✅[b] I have to praise choices that matter.[/b] There is reactivity to every choice you make—which big or small, can help or hinder you later in the game. I was incredibly pleased with the character creation first. There’s no basic hair or eye color or height. Instead, you can be male, female, or nonbinary. Incredibly, you can choose to be white, Indian, or Chinese. Other characters will actually react, negatively or positively to your choices. For example, I was a Chinese woman. Many people were incredibly confused at how I rose to my position of power. I was called a “celestial woman” with a tin star. But other Chinese immigrants asked for my advice, praising both my gender and race. Other bigots expressed their disbelief at me. The actual text responded to my race, as well: I could pipe up about Chinese foods, locations, and language. I even chose to be a doctor AND a lawyer, and folks commented on that too! This reactivity didn’t go away—it stayed throughout the game until the very end. 

✅ [b]RPG system.[/b][i] Tin Star[/i] isn’t a linear simple visual novel—I would argue it’s practically an RPG. During and after each chapter, you have an interlude. You have little “side missions” and lore conversations. You can literally walk up the town’s blacksmith and ask for his story. (You can skip these, but they're useful for improving your stats and opinions). You can build your own house, fix up your office, play chess with an RO, grow wealthy, and have brawls or gun fights. There’s a surprising amount of strategy for bigger conflicts, like group fights or diplomacy or flanking the enemy.

➡️ [b]Freedom and player agency.[/b] Let me give you an example. (Minor story spoilers here, but it’s no big mystery.) [spoiler]When travelling, you encounter a cowboy and a prospector engaged in a shootout. You first choose how you want to arrive at the scene and how to engage with both characters. You can go in guns blazing, shoot before asking questions, or lend an ear to the men and find out what’s really going on. This is your first chance to act as a marshall. Listen to both sides of the story. Choose who’s in the wrong or right and even decide who pays reparations. I repeat: you can kill both these men.[/spoiler] Oh, these are not some random NPCs. These are two major characters, one being an RO. There’s also another (female) RO you can [spoiler]kill[/spoiler] because she’s breaking the law. Again, the player agency is unmatched. You almost always have the option to say “♥♥♥♥ it,” pull your pistol out, and start shooting. 

✅ [b]Writing.[/b] The writing in [i]Tin Star[/i] is doing an insane amount of historical heavy lifting. There’s so much real knowledge baked in—about the Gold Rush, railroads, bandits, Mormon settlements, Native tribes, Chinese railroad workers, early banking, guns—you name it. But it never turns into a textbook. All of that context shows up exactly where it matters: in conversations, investigations, or why people are angry or desperate or dangerous. The game is not black or white; it's a lot of grey, as well.

✅ [b]Stat system. [/b]Usually I don’t like so many stats, and Tin Star has 12 main skills. However, the game gives you so many opportunities to improve them over time. There’s also a whopping 9 relationship bars with many minor characters. Order, Law, and Honor are also tracked. My favorite thing was how flavor text of stats changes as you advance a skill. So my gunfighting skill went from “Pull the trigger to make a lot of noise" to "There may be one person who can equal your lightning fast hands, and you haven’t met them yet." It makes you feel like you're actually progressing and building on a character. I checked the stat page many times—for fun.

✅[b] Epilogue.[/b] [i]Tin Star [/i]has one of the best epilogues ever due to its length. Usually, most IFs shy away from looking at the future. But [i]Tin Star[/i] says “♥♥♥♥ that” and includes a Legend system. Basically, all the noteworthy events you do are tracked and listed in the epilogue. So I have the fact that I never took a bribe; that I had books written about me; that I used a bear skin hide as a rug; that I saved the town from flooding, etc. I had four pages of summary! Oh, but of course Gies, the mad lad didn’t stop there. Bro had futures for major and minor characters—at least 16, in total. Even places I encountered had endings. For fun, I adopted a mouse as a pet. You betcha, my mouse had a happy ending with kids who somehow remembered me. What the hell, dude? I could go on, but this review is already too long. Just play this game.

[b][h2]Cons:[/h2][/b]
🟥 [b]More save spots.[/b] I love that [i]Tin Star [/i]has a checkpoint save system at the beginning/end of a chapter. However, I got killed by a bear multiple times (long story) and ended up having to replay 15 minutes of a chapter. The chapters get longer, as well. 

🟥 [b]Couple noticeable typos and odd paragraph breaks.[/b]

Best interactive fiction game ever! While also being engaging, emotional and entertaining, it also has some inclusions that make it one of the smoothest and least frustrating interactive fiction games I've played. If you die it asks you if you want to go back to one of four checkpoints, instead of just completely ending the game there. 

I also really loved the ending of how you can see all the characters lives play out after the ending (Kevin the blacksmith!! I'm so sorry i didn't stop in to see you everyday :( ). Sometimes you could tell that your actions may have made you skip over something that was important to the lore. I often found myself a little confused why everyone else seemed fine with a revelation I just found out. 

There isn't a lot of romancing included. However I didn't go down that path with the one character I did find a romance path for, cause I was waiting to see if there were more romance-able characters, so I cannot speak to the romance of it. I would love to play this game again one day and go down the romance path, but I also loved the way my game ended and am quite content with it. 

I became very invested in every characters life and would be terrified that one of them would die due to my actions (thankfully they didn't). I also found that, unlike other interactive fiction games (looking at you siege of Treboulain),  actions relating to skills aren't a fail or pass system. There were degrees of success and failure which allowed you to choose actions you felt were justified for the circumstance rather than just what your character was maxed out on. My character was horrible at brawling yet still was able to survive fights because I chose actions that I felt would work, I didn't destroy the other characters or anything but there were layers to an actions and subsequent actions that could back up your choice. I also LOVED that you had multiple chances to roam around the town. I would have liked to been able to interact with the main characters more in this section but that is truly a very small detail I'm only thinking about know. Anyway, I loved this one and I'm sure you will too!

Amazing choose-your-own-adventure game, it's cheaper than a real book but has twice the reading value. Your start is flexible, you have a lot of options and every stat affects something, nothing is useless. The changing flavor-text as you advance a skill is especially satisfying, going from "can barely hit the broadside of a barn" to "can shoot a flea a yard away" makes you feel like you're actually progressing and building on a character.

There's a broad cast of characters, and while not all of them are super interesting, there's enough interesting characters to keep you reading. The word-count doesn't lie, either, even if you don't read everything and skim some parts you'll get a 6-8 hour experience.

The epilogue is very much worth seeing too, you'll find out every character's path, from the majors to the minors, and it genuinely feels like your actions move the world around you.

Pick it up, on or off sale, it's worth the price tag.

Easily my favorite text-based game I've played (admittedly, a low bar to clear, since they are so few and far between.)

The story is remarkably multi-faceted. Chapters really do change their flow depending on what choices you make, however, each playthrough will hit the same narrative beats. To put it in a better way, i's a bit like Mass Effect, in the sense that your choices do shape the flow of the story in between the major, "locked-in" points in the narrative. Companions can also die/try to kill you depending on your actions and stance with each of them throughout critical points in the story. My lover in one playthrough tried to kill me in the next, on account of my earlier, different choices that I made.

My favorite thing about the game is being able to craft your personal legend. The number of legendary actions you commit to will influence how your character is remembered after the story. You can choose to be a stone-cold Steve Austin of a US Marshal, with dead-eye accuracy and lightning shooting from your fingertips (I'm being serious about that last part), or a mundane, run of the mill lawman/woman, there to do your job and little else throughout your tenure.

8/10, is admittedly a little boring, requires a lot of reading, and could have done with some ambiance or sound effects, but for the multi-faceted narrative alone, I have to recommend this game to anyone who thinks they're even a LITTLE bit interested.

Well written western saga that I will someday dust off and head out for another journey.

The Story:
You're recruited to be the new marshal in an unusual way. As marshal you have the choice to resolve a bunch of conflicts between the npcs or ignore them. Most of these conflicts will play into a larger overarching story. 
There's many different ways you can play your marshal: good, bad, lawful, rebel and anywhere in between. The game doesn't punish you for playing how you want to play.

Pros:
-Wealth system.
-12 skills. So many opportunities to improve them over time, but you can't master everything in one playthrough. 
-You can choose to save the chapter before moving onto the next.
-9 relationship bars, but also many minor characters. Many opportunities to improve them over time. 
-Many side missions and lore conversations. You can skip these, but they're useful for improving your stats and options.  
-Gun fights and brawls are great. A lot of options and different ways to resolve things. Great tension. 
-Diplomacy was done really well. 
-Multiple group fights. Surprises and different strategies. 
-Playing chess was done really well. Each round you and your opponent will pick between multiple strategies. 
-Town building. 
-Summary of your playthrough at the end. 

Cons:
-Ending was wrapped up too quickly. 
-Every character, no matter how minor, has an epilogue. I would have preferred a more detailed ending about what happens to my character. 

Final Verdict:
I'm not a big fan of westerns, but this was well thought out and there's a ton of choice. It's worth full price.

I've played a number of these text adventure games, and not just from Hosted. They've been somewhat of a passion of mine; the idea of controlling a story is a great one, and a text based game allows for more depth in every choice whereas other games may not.

That being said, Tin Star is one of the greatest "choose your own adventure" games I have ever played. The claim that this game has over a million words sounds like there will be long, boring paragraphs of unnessesary flavor text, but that's not the case at all.

Sure, the game can be long winded, but only when describing an important scene. Words aren't thrown about carelessly and are used to craft the expierence at nearly every turn. This game is long in the best way, always dropping new and intriguing characters and challenges for you to overcome as the Marshal of Lander County. It's great, and don't let that long word count put you off. There is a lot of GREAT content to be had here.

That said, the story itself it stellar. Without spoiling much, you are the new Federal Marshal of Lander County, a wild western place out around Nevada. You will face a multitude of interesting problems, facing off with interesting villians, making great friends, battling the elements, and truly role-playing your own character. 

I'm serious when I say this is a true RPG. You create your own backstory and name; they don't make you play as a pre-existing character like some of them. You can be as mean or kind as you want, as persuasive, intimidating, or deceptive as you want. You can use your head, friends, or just your guns to overcome you problems. You have stats to level that affect things, hundreds of choices, big and small, that affect who you are, how people thinkg about you, and how the world changes. I have NEVER seen this much freedom in one of these games. Sure, the progression of the story is linear, as you will always face the same setpieces in the same order, but you have so much freedome when it comes to tackling everything.

I mean, when dealing with potentially dangerous situations, you almost always have the option to just say "♥♥♥♥♥♥" and pull your pistol and start shooting. You could talk everyone down, or try to, but why do that when your choice of four or five pistols is hanging on your hip? Hell, I'm fairly certain you can kill half the named characters in the game by just shooting them when you first meet, and I'm not talking about the bad guys!

I can't recommend Tin Star enough if you are a fan of these games, and if you aren't a fan, this will make you one. Go play it, and become the sheriff you want to be. It's awesome.
